factual_errors: Section 10 claims the policy 'would authorize none of six historical direct-high dispatches as high', but Section 5.4's last bullet makes 'the main agent already uses high' a sufficient high trigger. The claim holds only if all six ran under a non-high main profile; as written it is unsupported and false for any case where the main agent was high.

Section 9's change estimate is internally inconsistent with its own surface list: Build wiring + Review wiring + extended frontmatter test + new focused prose-contract tests is only 'three existing files modified' if the new tests live inside the extended test file, which is not stated.

Section 9 refers to 'all four agent frontmatter files' while the evidence paths list only two stations (Build, Review). The count of four is asserted nowhere else and cannot be reconciled from the text.

Evidence path description mismatch: `test_agent_model_frontmatter.py` is described as the 'current prohibition on static effort pins'. A model-frontmatter test enforcing an effort prohibition is at minimum mislabeled, and Section 9 depends on that scope when it says 'extend the existing frontmatter test'.
judgment_calls: Model-first over effort-first for complex work is defensible, but the stated rationale ('it pays twice before observing whether the stronger model was sufficient') assumes a model step costs less than an effort step. On many hosts a frontier-tier step costs more than one effort step on the incumbent model, so the ordering is a preference, not a cost derivation.
'Crossing multiple files alone is not complex' is a reasonable anti-inflation bright line but will misclassify wide refactors with coupled invariants.

Refusing a persistent dispatch ledger keeps scope small but forecloses the controlled same-input comparison Section 10 says is still owed; accepting this means accepting that the efficacy claim stays unmeasurable in-band.
Folding review, blind runs, and probes into 'ordinary' at 0/0 trades systematic under-routing of adjudicative review for resistance to role-name inflation.
Treating routing as a pure optimization that may always degrade to the main agent is acceptable only because Section 6 forbids claiming the stronger profile ran.
contradictions_or_non_executable_transit: Section 2 permits `model_tier: inherit` and `effort: inherit`, but Sections 3-4 require ordinal arithmetic ('model -1', 'effort +1') and clamping to declared minimum and maximum. No arithmetic is defined on `inherit`, so classification is non-executable for a legal input.

'Rejected options' rejects an absolute standard/medium default because 'it discards a user-selected strong-model/low-effort baseline', yet Section 4's mechanical rule maps a user-selected frontier/high directly to standard/medium - the same discard, on two axes at once.

'Ambiguous debugging' is a complex signal while 'the observable packet cannot support one of the above' is insufficient-evidence with strictly higher precedence. Ambiguity is evidence for both classes with no tiebreak, so precedence silently converts most genuinely ambiguous complex work to main 0/0.

Section 6 branches on 'unsupported/rejected routing parameters' with no detection rule and no way to distinguish that condition from an ordinary execution error; with `supports_*_override: unknown` this is the common path, so the transition is not executable.
Section 6 retries with both overrides omitted even when only one was rejected; there is no partial-rejection branch, so a supported override is discarded without cause.
Section 7 selects FALLBACK_TO_MAIN vs FALLBACK_TO_HOST_DEFAULT from `guarantees_parent_inheritance`, but that field has an `unknown` value with no mapping.

Section 2's 'main profile cannot be observed -> omit both overrides' path has no outcome in Section 7's bounded enum: nothing was routed and no fallback was triggered, so `fallback_triggered: false` with `effective_profile: host-default/unverified` maps to no legal `outcome`.

Section 5 escalation is 'one cause at a time', but cause 2 ('raise model one tier, preserving effort') has no defined behavior when the model is already frontier; the ladder dead-ends instead of advancing to cause 3.
Section 5.3 caps escalated effort at 'initially no higher than medium' without defining when 'initially' ends, leaving an undefined transition from medium to high that bypasses the 5.4 trigger list.
false_downgrade_risks: frontier/high -> standard/medium for mechanical work drops both axes at once against an explicitly user-chosen baseline; one misclassification costs two steps with no pre-execution guard.

The mechanical class treats 'mechanical verification' as proof of low difficulty. Codemods, wide renames, and migrations pass mechanical verification while breaking invariants the verifier does not check; economy tier passes the gate and fails the intent.

'Ordinary' is the catch-all and includes review; combined with the rule that role and round names are not evidence, adjudicative review rounds route at main 0/0 by default and recover only through Section 5 escalation, i.e. after a weak review already exists.
insufficient-evidence outranking complex guarantees that the hardest, least-specified tasks run at the unadjusted main profile.
No floor ties the economy tier to work that ships user-visible behavior; a host mapping economy to a very weak model degrades output while the record still reports ROUTED.
false_upgrade_risks: The complex signal list ('cross-module reasoning', 'design trade-off', 'irreversible architecture', 'evidence conflict') is broad and the evidence is read from a dispatch packet the orchestrator itself authors; nothing adversarially checks the classification, so +1 model is effectively self-authorizing.

'The main agent already uses high' as a standalone high trigger contradicts the decision statement's 'evidence-only high effort': whenever the user sets high, every subagent inherits high with zero task evidence - the blanket high-use pattern the role-profile option was rejected for.
Model-first escalation makes frontier the default landing tier for anything labeled complex, including from a standard/low baseline where the user's choice signalled cost sensitivity.

Section 5's escalation causes are cheap to assert after any imperfect result ('shallow, unsupported, or unresolved reasoning' is a judgment with no observable test), so the ladder can be climbed on subjective dissatisfaction rather than evidence.
structured_output.fallback_assessment: Yes for the paths it defines: every Section 6 branch terminates in continue or EXECUTION_FAILED, retry is bounded at one, and no branch surfaces a model, effort, retry, or fallback choice to the user. The guarantee is incomplete rather than wrong, and three holes must be closed before it holds in practice: (a) the trigger 'unsupported/rejected routing parameters' has no detection rule, so an implementer will either over-trigger on generic errors or under-trigger and surface a raw failure to the user; (b) partial rejection of one override has no branch and currently discards the supported one; (c) the Section 2 unobservable-profile path exits routing without a legal outcome value, escaping the fallback machine rather than being handled by it. The terminal states EXECUTION_FAILED, NON_CONVERGENT, and REQUIREMENT_BLOCKED do reach the user, but they are work-product decisions, not routing decisions, so they do not break the claim.
smallest_required_changes: Define `inherit` and `unknown` as unobservable: any `inherit` in `main_profile` routes to the Section 2 omit-both path, and `guarantees_parent_inheritance: unknown` maps to FALLBACK_TO_HOST_DEFAULT. Two sentences.
Add one outcome value (e.g. `NOT_ROUTED`) for the Section 2 unobservable-profile case, or state explicitly that it records FALLBACK_TO_HOST_DEFAULT with `fallback_triggered: false`.

Add a mechanical-downgrade floor: mechanical adjusts at most one axis, or never reduces effort below the main profile when the main effort was explicitly user-set. This removes the contradiction with the rejected-options rationale.

Give one concrete tiebreak between 'ambiguous debugging' (complex) and insufficient-evidence - e.g. insufficient-evidence applies only when the packet lacks a goal or checkable acceptance condition, not when the subject matter is ambiguous.
State the observable signal that counts as 'unsupported/rejected routing parameters' and the rule for partial rejection (retry with only the rejected override omitted).
Add the missing escalation transition: when cause 2 applies and the model is already frontier, advance to cause 3 instead of stopping.
Bound 'initially no higher than medium' with a concrete condition for lifting the cap (only via a Section 5.4 trigger), so no undefined medium-to-high path exists.
Restate the Section 10 claim as 'none of six would be authorized as high on task evidence alone', and report the main profile of those six so the inheritance trigger is accounted for.
Correct the Section 9 file count and the described scope of `test_agent_model_frontmatter.py`.
delete_instead_of_expand: Section 9's '100-145 maintained lines' estimate together with the sentence saying it must be replaced by actual diff counts - a self-invalidating number that will be wrong either way; delete both rather than refine.
The `fallback_policy: omit-both-overrides-once` field in Section 8 - a constant restating policy, not an observation; the record should hold only observed values.

One of FALLBACK_TO_MAIN / FALLBACK_TO_HOST_DEFAULT: they are distinguished solely by a host capability flag that is frequently `unknown`. Collapse to a single FALLBACK outcome with `inheritance_guaranteed: true|false|unknown` in the record.
'The main agent already uses high' as a Section 5.4 escalation trigger - inheritance is already handled by Section 4.5, so listing it as an evidence trigger only weakens the evidence-only rule.
The `risk_signals` and `failure_trajectory` empty-list fields in Section 2 unless a populating rule is added; as written they are unused inputs that invite retrofitted justification.
